blocks.content: You know how a sorted array lets you binary search in O(log n), but a sorted linked list makes you crawl through every single node one by one just to find one value?

The linked list has all the right data in exactly the right order, but it gives you none of the speed. There's no way to jump to the middle of a linked list the way you jump to the middle index of an array, because a node only knows about the node right next to it.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785306139336-526043784.png
blocks.alt: Sorted linked list requiring a full linear scan to reach a target value

blocks.content: Skip lists fix this. They take a plain sorted linked list and bolt express lanes on top of it, so you can skip over large chunks of the list instead of visiting every single node. And the wild part is how they decide where those express lanes go: with a coin flip.
A skip list is a sorted linked list with a randomized index built on top of it, giving you tree like search speed without ever needing to rebalance anything.
1. Introduction

Say you're maintaining a leaderboard, a priced order book, or any sorted set that needs frequent inserts, deletes, and range lookups. You want the whole thing to stay sorted at all times, and you want search, insert, and delete to all be fast, not just one of them.

A sorted array gives you fast search through binary search, but insert and delete are slow because you have to shift elements to keep everything contiguous. A plain linked list gives you fast insert and delete once you've found the spot, but finding the spot means walking from the front every time.

Balanced trees like AVL trees and red black trees solve this properly, with O(log n) search, insert, and delete, all guaranteed. But look at what it costs to actually implement one. Rotations, balance factors, color flips, and a long list of edge cases around rebalancing after every single insert and delete. That's a lot of code and a lot of ways to introduce a subtle bug.

Skip lists get you the same expected O(log n) time for search, insert, and delete, and they do it with a data structure that's genuinely simple to write and reason about. No rotations. No rebalancing logic. Just linked lists stacked on top of each other, with randomness doing the job that rotations do in a tree.

blocks.title: Why this matters
blocks.content: Skip lists show up in real production systems precisely because of this simplicity. Redis uses them for sorted sets, and several concurrent data structure libraries reach for them instead of balanced trees because they're far easier to make thread safe.
2. How a skip list works

Think about Mumbai's suburban trains. The slow train stops at every single station between two ends of the line. It gets you everywhere, but it's painfully slow if your destination is far off. The fast train skips dozens of small stations and only halts at the major ones, so if your destination happens to be a major station, you get there in a fraction of the time.

A skip list works like a rail network with several lines stacked over the same route. The bottom layer is the slow train: a regular sorted linked list that touches every element. Above it sit faster layers that skip over more and more nodes. The topmost layer might stop at only a handful of nodes across the entire list.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785306141579-561434801.png
blocks.alt: Skip list express layer skipping over nodes in the base linked list

blocks.content: To search for something, you start on the topmost, fastest layer and ride it as far as you can without passing your target. The moment continuing would overshoot, you drop down one layer to a slower train and repeat. You keep doing that until you land on the base layer, where you either find the value or confirm it isn't there.
2.1 The coin flip that builds the layers
blocks.text: 2.1 The coin flip that builds the layers

blocks.content: Here's the part that makes skip lists feel almost too simple: nobody decides ahead of time which nodes belong to which express layer. It gets decided by a coin flip, one node at a time, right when you insert it.

When you insert a new node, you flip a coin. Heads, you promote the node to the next layer up and flip again. Tails, you stop. So a node has roughly a fifty percent chance of existing only at the base layer, a twenty five percent chance of also reaching layer two, a twelve and a half percent chance of reaching layer three, and so on, halving each time.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785306145928-19960886.png
blocks.alt: Coin flip determining how many layers a new skip list node joins

blocks.content: Nobody is tracking balance factors. Nobody is rotating anything after the fact. The structure just tends toward a good shape because of how probability behaves, and that's really the whole trick behind skip lists.

blocks.title: Why coin flips instead of a fixed rule
blocks.content: A fixed rule, like promoting every second node, would need constant upkeep as you insert and delete, which brings back the same rebalancing headache trees have. Randomization spreads nodes across layers on average without anyone having to enforce it by hand.
2.2 Search

Searching starts at the top left corner of the structure, at the highest layer that currently exists. From there the whole algorithm boils down to two moves, repeated over and over: move right while the next node's value is still less than what you're looking for, and drop down a layer the moment moving right would overshoot.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396031002-350169946.png
blocks.alt: Skip list search moving right across a layer then dropping down after overshooting the target

blocks.content: ["Start at the highest layer, at the very first node.","If the next node at this layer has a value less than your target, move right.","If moving right would overshoot the target, or there's no next node, drop down one layer.","Repeat until you reach layer zero, then check whether the next node matches your target."]
items: Start at the highest layer, at the very first node.
If the next node at this layer has a value less than your target, move right.
If moving right would overshoot the target, or there's no next node, drop down one layer.
Repeat until you reach layer zero, then check whether the next node matches your target.

blocks.content: Every dead end at a high layer saves you from checking a whole run of nodes at the base layer that you now know can't matter.
2.3 Insert

Insertion starts exactly like a search. You walk down through the layers the same way, except this time you remember the last node you touched at each layer, the node right before where your target will land. These become your update pointers, one per layer.

Once you've found the insertion point at the base layer, flip your coin to decide how tall the new node should be. Then splice the new node in at every layer from the base up to that height, using the update pointers you collected on the way down.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785306150288-868286604.png
blocks.alt: New node spliced into both the base layer and a higher layer during insertion

blocks.content: If the coin flip gives the new node a height taller than any layer that currently exists, the skip list simply grows a new top layer, with the header pointing straight to the new node on that layer.
2.4 Delete

Delete is insertion in reverse. Walk down collecting the update pointers the same way you would for a search. When you reach the target node at the base layer, unlink it at every layer it appears on by pointing each update pointer's next reference around it.

If removing the node happens to leave the top layer empty, you lower the skip list's tracked height by one. That's the entire cleanup. No rebalancing pass, no fixup routine, nothing cascading back up the structure.

blocks.title: Gotcha: don't forget the height check
blocks.content: If you skip lowering the skip list's max height when the top layers empty out, you'll waste time walking through empty layers on every future search. It's a small detail, but it's the most common bug people leave sitting in a skip list implementation.
3. Why randomization gives you O log n without rebalancing
blocks.text: 3. Why randomization gives you O log n without rebalancing

blocks.content: With a coin flip that promotes a node to the next layer with probability one half, the expected number of layers a skip list needs for n elements works out to roughly log base two of n. That's because the number of nodes present at each layer roughly halves as you go up, the same halving that makes binary search fast.

At each layer, the expected number of nodes you move right through before dropping down is a small constant, it doesn't grow with n. Stack up roughly log n layers, each costing constant work, and you land on expected O(log n) total work for search, insert, and delete.

blocks.title: Expected, not guaranteed
blocks.content: This is the one place skip lists genuinely differ from balanced trees. A red black tree guarantees O(log n) worst case, full stop. A skip list's O(log n) is an expected value, averaged over the randomness of the coin flips. In an extremely unlucky run, every node could technically land at the base layer only, degrading to O(n). With a proper random number generator this essentially never happens in practice.

Most implementations also cap the maximum number of layers based on the expected size of the data, so even a run of bad luck can only cost a bounded amount of extra work rather than spiraling unpredictably.
4. Worked example: a game leaderboard

Say you're building a leaderboard for a mobile game. Scores need to stay sorted at all times, new scores get inserted constantly, old ones get removed when a player's session ends, and the product wants a feature that shows every player's score within a chosen range, like everyone between rank ten and rank fifty.
4.1 Building the skip list

You start inserting scores as they come in: 350, then 610, then 420, then 390, then 500. Each insert walks down the existing layers to find its spot, then flips a coin to decide how tall it grows. Say 610 gets promoted all the way to the top layer, 350 also lands on that top layer, and the rest stay lower down.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785306152878-631578841.png
blocks.alt: Leaderboard skip list with an express layer connecting the highest and lowest scores

blocks.content: Notice the shape is entirely a byproduct of the coin flips. If you replayed the exact same inserts again, you'd probably end up with a different set of nodes on the express layer, and the leaderboard would still work exactly the same, just with a slightly different internal shape.
4.2 Range query for the leaderboard

Now a player wants to see everyone scoring between 400 and 550. You run a normal search for 400 using the express layers, which lands you at the right spot in the base layer in a handful of hops instead of scanning from the start. From there you just walk right along the base layer, collecting every node until you pass 550.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785306155443-606834280.png
blocks.alt: Range query walking along the base layer between two boundary scores

blocks.title: Range query result
blocks.text: Searching narrows you down to 420 in about three hops using the express layers instead of walking past every lower score one at a time. From there, a short walk right along the base layer collects 420 and 500, then stops as soon as it reaches 610, which is outside the requested range.

blocks.content: That combination, an O(log n) search to find the start of the range, followed by a plain O(k) walk along the base layer to collect k results, is exactly why skip lists are such a natural fit for range queries.
5. Implementation
Here's a working skip list in JavaScript covering search, insert, and delete. It's close to what you'd actually write in an interview or drop into a real project, minus any production hardening.

A few things worth pointing out. Each node stores a forward array sized to its own level, not to the skip list's overall maximum level, so short nodes don't waste memory on pointers they'll never use.

The update array collected during search doubles as the exact set of pointers you need to touch during insert or delete, which is why both operations start by running essentially the same walk as search.

The randomLevel function is the entire probabilistic engine. Swap the probability from one half to something else, like one quarter, and you trade a taller expected structure with fewer nodes per layer for a shorter one with more nodes per layer. One half is the common default because it balances layer count against per layer width reasonably well.
6. Skip lists versus balanced trees
Both structures give you expected or guaranteed O(log n) search, insert, and delete over sorted data, so the choice usually comes down to what you're optimizing for beyond raw asymptotics.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785306157799-691782182.png
blocks.alt: Skip list built from stacked linked layers compared against a balanced tree needing rotations

blocks.content: A balanced tree gives you a hard worst case guarantee and slightly better memory locality in some implementations, but every insert and delete can trigger a rotation, and writing that rotation logic correctly is genuinely fiddly. A skip list trades that hard guarantee for a much smaller, much easier to verify implementation, plus pointers that are simple to update without touching unrelated parts of the structure.

7. Real systems that use skip lists
blocks.text: 7. Real systems that use skip lists

blocks.content: Skip lists aren't just a textbook curiosity. Several widely used systems reach for them specifically because of the tradeoffs from the last section.
7.1 Redis sorted sets

Redis backs its sorted set data type with a skip list paired with a hash table. The hash table gives constant time lookup from a member to its score, and the skip list keeps every member ordered by score so commands like fetching a rank range or the top scores run in logarithmic time plus the size of the result.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785306160123-557368117.png
blocks.alt: Client sending a sorted set command to Redis, served internally by a skip list paired with a hash table

blocks.content: 7.2 LevelDB and RocksDB memtables

Both LevelDB and RocksDB buffer recent writes in memory before flushing them to disk as sorted files. That in memory buffer, called a memtable, is commonly implemented as a skip list, because it needs fast ordered insert, fast lookup, and easy in order iteration when it's time to flush everything to disk as a sorted run. A skip list gives all three without any rebalancing overhead sitting on the write path.
7.3 Concurrent and lock free skip lists
blocks.text: 7.3 Concurrent and lock free skip lists

blocks.content: Java's ConcurrentSkipListMap is a standard library example of a lock free ordered map, and it leans on skip lists rather than a balanced tree for a simple reason: splicing a new node into a linked layer only touches a couple of neighboring pointers, which plays nicely with compare and swap operations. Rebalancing a shared tree under concurrent writers, by contrast, can touch a much wider region of the structure at once, which is far harder to make safe without heavier locking.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785306162398-127549067.png
blocks.alt: Multiple reader threads traversing a skip list concurrently while a writer inserts a node

blocks.content: This is a big part of why skip lists show up in concurrent libraries far more often than balanced trees do. It's not that trees can't be made concurrent, it's that skip lists make it dramatically easier to get right.
8. The interview angle

If you're asked to design an ordered data structure that supports search, insert, delete, and range queries, and the interviewer pushes on concurrency or on how much code you'd realistically want to own and maintain, a skip list is a strong answer. It gets you the same asymptotic behavior as a balanced tree with far less implementation risk.

Be ready to state the tradeoff honestly rather than overselling it: you're trading a guaranteed worst case for an expected one, in exchange for a much simpler structure. Interviewers tend to respond well when you say that out loud instead of implying skip lists are strictly better than trees in every situation.
